initial.summary:
Passive reconnaissance on paypal.com was performed using WHOIS and VirusTotal; the Wayback Machine source was unavailable (HTTP 503 on two attempts) and therefore contributed no evidence either way.

1. VERDICT
- Risk level: LOW (benign)
- Nature of domain: paypal.com is the primary, long-established domain of PayPal, a major global payment provider
- Analyst note: the "suspicious" flag is not supported by any collected evidence; it is most plausibly explained by brand-abuse context (paypal.com is one of the most impersonated brands in phishing), not by the domain itself

2. WHOIS / REGISTRAR EVIDENCE
- Creation date: 1999-07-15 — over 26 years of registration history, strongly inconsistent with a throwaway phishing domain
- Registrar: MarkMonitor Inc. — a corporate brand-protection registrar typically used by large enterprises
- Expiration: 2027-07-15 — long renewal horizon, no sign of short-lived/abuse-style registration
- Registrant country: US; registrant org redacted for privacy (standard for MarkMonitor corporate clients)
- Abuse contact: abusecomplaints@markmonitor.com — a dedicated, monitored abuse channel
- Domain status: client/server Delete, Transfer and Update Prohibited — full lock set, typical of high-value corporate assets
- Name servers: NS1/NS2-PCHNET.PAYPAL.COM (in-bailiwick, brand-owned) plus PDNS100.ULTRADNS.COM/.NET — enterprise-grade DNS with redundancy
- DNSSEC: signed / signedDelegation — DNSSEC enabled, a hygiene control rarely seen on malicious infrastructure

3. VIRUSTOTAL REPUTATION AND PASSIVE DNS
- Reputation score: 60 (positive)
- Engine verdicts: 59 harmless, 0 malicious, 0 suspicious, 33 undetected
- Community votes: 7 harmless vs 1 malicious — the single malicious vote is an outlier against 59 clean engines and is not actionable
- Categories: none assigned (no security-vendor categorization as malicious)
- Passive DNS: long, coherent history from 2013 to 2025 across known CDN/edge ranges (151.101.x, 162.159.x, 192.229.x) and legacy PayPal-owned ranges (64.4.250.x, 173.0.8x.x, 173.224.x) — consistent with a large legitimate operator migrating between CDNs, not with fast-flux abuse

4. WAYBACK MACHINE
- Status: unavailable — CDX API returned HTTP 503 on both attempts
- Interpretation: source-side outage, not evidence of absence of history; given the 1999 creation date, an extensive archive history is expected
- Impact: does not weaken the verdict, since WHOIS and VirusTotal independently and strongly support legitimacy

5. CORROBORATION ACROSS SOURCES
- All three weighted signals that could be collected point the same way: aged domain, brand-protection registrar, locked status, DNSSEC, zero malicious engine detections, positive reputation
- No conflicting indicator was observed in any collected dataset

6. CAVEATS
- This assessment covers the apex domain paypal.com only; it says nothing about lookalike/typosquat domains, subdomains, or URLs that merely contain the string "paypal"
- The original analyst alert likely concerns a URL, email or page impersonating PayPal rather than this domain itself
initial.risk_justification: The verdict rests on a convergent body of evidence, not a single signal. WHOIS shows paypal.com created 1999-07-15 (26+ years old), registered through MarkMonitor (corporate brand-protection registrar), locked with the full client/server Delete-Transfer-Update Prohibited set, DNSSEC-signed, with brand-owned in-bailiwick name servers plus UltraDNS — a profile essentially incompatible with malicious or disposable infrastructure. VirusTotal corroborates: reputation 60, 59 engines harmless, 0 malicious, 0 suspicious, and a passive DNS history spanning 2013-2025 across known CDN and legacy PayPal-owned ranges, consistent with a large legitimate operator. The only negative datapoint is a single malicious community vote against 7 harmless votes and 59 clean engines, which is an outlier and not actionable. Wayback was unavailable (HTTP 503 twice), so it contributed no evidence; however, the two independent sources that did respond are both strongly benign, so the missing source does not create meaningful uncertainty. The analyst's "suspicious" flag is best explained by PayPal being a heavily impersonated brand, i.e. the risk lies in lookalike domains and phishing URLs, not in paypal.com itself.
recommendations: Treat paypal.com as a legitimate, benign domain and close the alert on the apex domain itself; do not block or sinkhole it.

Re-scope the investigation to the actual artifact that triggered the alert (full URL, sender address, redirect chain, or page content) — the threat is almost certainly impersonation of PayPal, not PayPal's own domain.

Check for lookalike/typosquat domains (e.g. paypa1.com, paypal-secure.*, paypal.com.<other-tld>) and for subdomains or paths hosted on third-party infrastructure that merely contain the string 'paypal'.

If a suspicious URL was reported, verify the registrable domain in the URL bar rather than the display text or the presence of 'paypal' anywhere in the string, and inspect the certificate issuer for the actual host.
Re-run the Wayback Machine lookup later to complete the evidence set; the 503 was a source-side outage and its absence should not be read as a negative finding.

Remind users that PayPal never requests credentials, card numbers or one-time codes by email or unsolicited call, and route suspected phishing to the abuse contact abusecomplaints@markmonitor.com and to PayPal's own phishing reporting channel.
